title: The Pacific Is a Mess of Hurricanes
excerpt: If you could look down at the Pacific Ocean right now, you’d see three hurricanes spinning in a row, between 15 and 20 degrees north
body: If you could look down at the Pacific Ocean right now, you’d see three hurricanes spinning in a row, between 15 and 20 degrees north
Furthest east is Polo, an unusually strong hurricane that has been churning off the southern coast of Mexico for nearly a week
To its west, Odalys, once a Category 4 hurricane, is slowly weakening in the open ocean

In the central Pacific, Hurricane Nolo has reached Category 2 status and has crept about 145 miles off the coast of Hawaii’s Big Island, where it’s expected to bring up to 25 inches of rain, potentially causing flooding and landslides
The ocean is a mess of hurricanes, and it’s not the first time this season
Just last month, four storms formed across the Pacific over a 12-day period
Two of them, Hurricane Lala and Tropical Storm Moke, came dangerously close to Hawaii
Driven by an exceptional El Niño event, these tropical storms have increased in frequency compared with an average year
Typically, at this point in the season, 12 tropical storms would have formed in the eastern Pacific, Michael Brennan, the director of the National Hurricane Center, told me
Of the storms in the Pacific now, Polo, which has wobbled between Category 4 and 5, is the monster, and it will likely bring catastrophic damage when it makes landfall on Monday

The warm water temperatures associated with El Niño increase the likelihood of stronger storms, and this year’s event is shaping up to be one of the most dramatic on record . “El Niño is the ‘great nudger’ of weather systems around the planet,” Michelle L’Heureux, who leads the El Niño–Southern Oscillation team at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Climate Prediction Center, wrote in an email. “Very strong El Niños are often able to nudge more.” Warmer waters also mean that the area where a storm can form expands
Storms tend to show up in the region where Polo is lingering, Brennan said, and generally, by the time they reach the central part of the ocean, near Hawaii, they weaken
But this year, waters in the central Pacific are more than 3 degrees Celsius warmer than usual, allowing hurricanes such as Nolo to form south of the islands and much closer to them
When I asked Brennan how abnormal this was—I’d seen others calling this a historic hurricane season—he said that a season like this comes around every decade or so
Nolo is only the latest in a string of disasters that the island of Hawaii has endured this year
In January, the Kilauea volcano erupted for eight hours, and blanketed communities on the island with rocks and ash
Then, back-to-back Kona lows, a type of seasonal cyclone, brought historic flooding in March
Two months later, a 6.0-magnitude earthquake shook the island and damaged nearly 150 homes
In mid-August, Hurricane Lala, a Category 1 storm, dumped some 30 inches of rain on parts of the Big Island without making landfall
David Ho, a professor of oceanography at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, was at home in Honolulu when Lala hit
His neighborhood flooded, and he was one of 200,000 electricity customers across the state who lost power

More than 200 homes and an estimated $67 million worth of public infrastructure were damaged, according to the Hawaii Emergency Management Agency. “We have a lot of houses that were built before the building codes were modernized,” Ho told me. “So once in a while, you have roofs that just fly away.” Weeks later, many people, especially those in rural areas with limited access to groceries, are still feeling Lala’s lingering effects. “We always talk about the importance of being prepared, and you want to have three weeks of food supply and everything,” Janice Ikeda, the CEO of the nonprofit Vibrant Hawaii, told me. “Well, we don’t have that anymore, because it got wiped out.” (The state reissued Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits to more than 65,000 households after the storm.) The damage and losses the island suffered from Lala only make lives and infrastructure more vulnerable in the face of Nolo

For even one storm to skirt that close to Hawaii would have been an event: The Pacific Ocean is big enough, and the Hawaiian Islands are small enough, that most hurricanes roll by at a much greater distance
But earlier this month, another storm, Lowell, approached the western part of the state, near Kauai and Niihau, pushing hurricane-strength winds and waves ashore
More than 90 percent of utility customers in Kauai lost power
Nolo likely won’t be a repeat of Lala or Lowell, because it is farther out and should remain 100 miles from the coast, Brennan said
Even so, the island could see more than two feet of rain, coastal flooding, and high surf
The hurricane season doesn’t end for another two months, and the effect of El Niño is likely to only get stronger, according to NOAA’s current predictions
Before the year is through, the “great nudger” will likely hurl more hurricanes Hawaii’s way
In the Atlantic, the nudge is working in the opposite direction: El Niño generates strong wind shears, which make it hard for hurricanes to form
September should mark the peak of the Atlantic hurricane season, Allison Wing, an associate professor of atmospheric science at Florida State University, told me
Nearly four months into hurricane season, no hurricanes have appeared, and none are on the horizon.

title: What Israel Knew Before October 7
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Less than two weeks before October 7, 2023, Egypt’s top spy flew to Israel to deliv
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Less than two weeks before October 7, 2023, Egypt’s top spy flew to Israel to deliver a dire warning: Hamas appeared to be mobilizing for a major attack

According to officials who spoke with the Atlantic staff writer Vivian Salama, Cairo’s intelligence chief recommended that the Israeli government offer economic concessions to Hamas in order to avert conflict
What Israeli officials did with that warning remains an open question three years after the most devastating surprise attack in the country’s history
On this episode of Radio Atlantic , Salama says officials from seven different countries told her that the visit should have set off alarms across the top ranks of the Israeli government

The following is a transcript of the episode: Adam Harris: I’m Adam Harris, and I’m here in the PBS studios of Washington Week With The Atlantic for a special taping of Radio Atlantic , with Atlantic staff writer Vivian Salama
You have some new, exclusive reporting, and the headline of the story is “Egypt’s Warning to Israel.” It’s about the October 7th attack

What did you find out about the October 7th attack? Vivian Salama: Adam, we’re coming up on the third anniversary of the tragic attacks of October 7th, and I set out several months ago to try to understand exactly what was known

I was starting to get bits and pieces of information from sources about possible warnings that came in advance of it—easy to dismiss on its face because Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and most of his government have denied that there were prior warnings ahead of the tragedy
But the more I looked into it and the more people I talked to, I realized a very peculiar incident that happened exactly on September 26th, 2023

And the reason this date was so significant and really stood out is because that was the day that the government held a very large 50th-anniversary commemoration of the Yom Kippur War: the war 50 years ago when, ironically, Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack on Israel
And the whole premise of his speech was essentially that we need to be prepared, that we wouldn’t turn a blind eye to the threats around us and to our adversaries
All the while, about two hours prior to Netanyahu taking the stage, a small Cessna jet arrived in Ben-Gurion Airport about 30 miles away from where Bibi was talking
I really had to dig deep and work for months to try to figure out who this Cessna belonged to
There had been some rumors and some tips that it belonged to the Egyptian security chief, the intelligence chief
But I really had to actually connect those dots and go down rabbit holes to try to really confirm that this was his plane; the flight plan was Cairo to Ben-Gurion

And what we found from multiple, multiple applications, but also the Israeli flight logs which we later discovered, is that that plane landed early that morning, kinda tucked away in this very restricted area at Ben-Gurion Airport, and stayed for about 67 minutes, according to the Israeli flight log

And through multiple sources, and I’m talking to people in Israel, in Egypt, across the Arab world, in Europe, and the United States, I managed to confirm that he was on that plane, the Egyptian intelligence chief
He was there, and he came with a very ominous message of danger in Gaza

And so he met with security officials in the Israeli government, some senior officials, and essentially conveyed to them what they saw, which was that there was mobilization for an unprecedented attack of some kind
But he knew that the situation was so grave
And for him to go to Israel for 67 minutes to deliver a message—that alone signified that the situation was so urgent and so grave

And so the question then became: What happened with the message? Typically something like this—just the sheer presence of the Egyptian intelligence chief would send off red flags across the Israeli government
My sources tell me that after Netanyahu finished his speech at the Yom Kippur ceremony, he went into a classified meeting
Some believe that he would’ve gotten the warning then; however, the Netanyahu government refused to answer my questions, and so it remains unclear if those warnings made it to him or not

Countless Israeli officials I talked to said, There is no world —literally, that’s a direct quote— There is no world in which the Egyptian spy chief comes to Israel for an hour to deliver a message , where likely the Egyptian president commissioned him to go, and Bibi doesn't know about that
And so the question then became: What more did they know? It seems clear, and even through U.S. officials, I later confirmed, that they had multiple warnings from the Egyptians
But in particular, within that two-week time frame of the October 7th attack, you had the visit from Abbas Kamel to Israel
You also had two written cables that went to them warning them of a possible attack
And so all of this is a collective body of evidence that really signaled that there was trouble brewing right on Israel’s doorstep
Harris: You’ve mentioned that the prime minister had denied that there were warnings before

Were there other warnings in addition to these that you’ve mentioned, that we have confirmed? Or were these the only warnings? Salama: So through months of investigating this, I was able to determine that the United Arab Emirates’ president, Mohamed bin Zayed, also picked up the phone probably the same day or around the same time as Abbas Kamel visited Israel
Now, that story, to the credit of Haaretz , the newspaper in Israel, they got that element of it out a couple of weeks ago and were able to report it
I have independently confirmed that the story’s absolutely correct
And my understanding through all my sources that I talked to is that that phone call was actually largely inspired by the Egyptian intelligence he received
I want to emphasize that when it comes to Gaza, there are two countries that basically have eyes on it, and that is Israel and Egypt

They have sources within the Strip, and they follow it very closely because both countries, despite all their differences, really view Hamas’s activity within the Strip as a security threat to both of their countries
And so they do work very closely on intelligence sharing when it comes to Gaza
And so for the Egyptian intel chief to travel to Israel—that is someone who knows what he’s talking about
But it also appears that Egypt dispersed that intelligence throughout the region, that officials in the region knew he traveled to Israel as well
And MBZ, Mohamed bin Zayed, was so disturbed by the findings he was hearing, both from the Egyptians and from his own Palestinian sources, that he picked up the phone and called Netanyahu directly

title: How to Define the Fuzzy Phases of Life

body: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight
Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning
When, exactly, does middle age begin and end? This past summer, my colleague Julie Beck tried to figure it out
Public opinion didn’t exactly offer a consensus: “In one survey , the median response put middle age as lasting from 40 to 60,” Beck writes
But The Wall Street Journal also reported a few years ago that 20 percent of people ages 25 to 34 claim they feel middle-aged

People tend to think about the term in relation to the age they currently are, Beck writes. “The older people are, the later they tend to think middle age starts and ends.” At a certain point in her quest to define the exact contours of middle age, “I started losing my grip a little,” Beck writes

The numbers were nearly impossible to pin down, and “ultimately, middle age might be better understood as a feeling that creeps up on you than as a clear turning point.” “It’s a time of life that is often both exhausting and fulfilling,” Beck notes: “when you’ve lived enough life to have learned some lessons, and also have plenty of time ahead of you to make changes.” That feeling may show up at 35, or 45, or 65
Perhaps all that matters is what we do with it when it arrives

title: Modern Media Weaken the Presidency
excerpt: Donald Trump’s second term represents a new, bolder version of the “imperial presidency” that many feared half a century ago
body: Donald Trump’s second term represents a new, bolder version of the “imperial presidency” that many feared half a century ago
Trump prefers a maximalist approach to presidential power
And the Supreme Court, by granting presidents immunity from most prosecution and subduing what were once thought of as independent agencies, has lent him some support
One might assume that the media have done so as well, albeit inadvertently—that as the news business has become weaker, the presidency has become stronger
Most local newspapers have collapsed in the hands of hedge funds and private equity; advertising has been gobbled up by digital platforms; tens of thousands of journalists have lost their job
Trump has used the press to his political advantage, often appearing omnipresent and dominant in the news
Last week, he banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House because of their critical coverage, in a seeming show of force
A judge has already blocked that legally dubious ban
What’s more, a closer look at the changes that have swept through the news business this century reveals that their tendency is to weaken the presidency, undermining Trump’s attempts to exert control
Individual journalists and publications continue to provide an important check on the president
Other structural forces in the industry have made the effective exercise of presidential power more difficult

The fragmentation of the media, with new forms, formats, and players continuing to mushroom, gives political actors more opportunities for narrowcasting—that is, reaching particular audiences with more precision than was previously possible

This was in evidence during the 2024 campaign, when Trump and then Kamala Harris devoted precious time to appearing on podcasts that they surely did not listen to and perhaps had not previously heard of
But narrowcasting, by its nature, seems less available to incumbents than to challengers

If a president says something notable, what happens on the podcast is not likely to stay there. [ Jonathan Chait: Trump’s attacks on the media are self-defeating ] Although the president can take advantage of his unique ability to broadcast a message to virtually the whole nation, broadcasting is becoming less effective
In the last four decades of the 20th century, an address televised in prime time was a powerful tool, especially for presidents skilled at using the medium, including John F
Since the Obama administration, a president who appears on “all of the networks” is far from appearing on all of the screens

Even as the national population has grown by about a third since Reagan’s presidency, audiences for Trump’s State of the Union speeches, for instance, have been markedly smaller than the audiences in the 1980s
Much of what would previously have been the president’s audience is occupied elsewhere, streaming or scrolling, and often focused on matters other than public affairs
A larger share of voters today receives the president’s message only after it has been mediated by reporters, commentators, or social-media users
This would have been a significant detriment to the likes of Franklin D

Trump uses social media to powerful and unprecedented effect; it is the vehicle that he turns to, more than any other, to redirect the national conversation, often employing it to announce major policy and personnel moves
Still, social media is a deeply imperfect substitute for what TV used to be, from the perspective of presidential power
First, the short-form nature of social media encourages messages that are telegraphic rather than educational, making it an instrument of announcement more than persuasion
Second, social media makes it very easy for the people sharing messages to also interpret them
Not only has intermediation, long a frustration of presidents, increased, but far fewer of the mediators are journalists
All of this has likely weakened the president’s once-celebrated ability to “teach” the country, in the manner of FDR during his fireside chats
For his February 1942 chat, about the tough early days of World War II, Roosevelt asked Americans to consult a map of the world as they listened

A president seeking to do this kind of teaching today would find that the “pupils” he most wanted to reach were those least likely to tune in, and that his “lessons” were being filtered and colored for many recipients (and by many)
An exception to this trend may exist for moments of genuine crisis, but presidents must seize the occasion and be disciplined in doing so
Trump’s daily appearances during the coronavirus pandemic in March and April 2020, which unraveled quickly and then were discontinued, show how easily such a moment can be squandered

One countervailing force is that when the press, particularly cable television, becomes more partisan, media actors can command loyalty to the president by intimidating other officials in his party into supporting him and his policies
Right-leaning media outlets have certainly helped Trump dominate Republican primary elections
But the same phenomenon all but guarantees a permanent opposition faction in the press, which can at times be just as strong as the supportive faction, if not more so

A partisan press also sharply limits a president’s ability to forge consensus, or even to seek compromise, which he needs in order to legislate with lasting effect. [ Read: The press is not the root of Trump’s problems ] One of the most profound ways that the news business has changed in this century is the nationalization of much of what passes for news, despite how deeply Americans still care about what’s happening in their local communities
Simply put, less local news is being produced, more local events are going unobserved, and national news often fills the void
Members of Congress who might once have heard at town halls about primarily district-level matters now find themselves buffeted by countrywide worries
For presidents, this seems, at best, a mixed blessing
When a president has events moving in his favor, the effect may be strengthened at the local level
Yet this same dynamic can exaggerate the effect when voters are unhappy with the state of the country—a secular trend at least in the past decade or more

title: How Militarizing the Triumphal Arch Could Backfire for Trump
excerpt: Donald Trump’s vision for a monumental arch in the nation’s capital was always ambitious
body: Donald Trump’s vision for a monumental arch in the nation’s capital was always ambitious
He has called for a 250-foot structure clad in granite, with gilded winged statues, an observation deck, a café, a gift shop, and an exhibition space—all to be completed by the end of his second term
And that was before he decided that the “triumphal arch” should also be a military complex
Since the project was announced last year, the Trump administration has raced to begin work on the memorial, checking many of the boxes required of a major new building project in D.C
It cleared one key panel, the Commission of Fine Arts, which Trump has stacked with loyalists
It got a sign-off from the Federal Aviation Administration (which has called for a “non-standard eternal flame” on the arch so that pilots can see it at night)

Although the project still faces a lawsuit filed by veterans and a preservationist, this week an obscure independent federal agency terminated the project’s ongoing historic-preservation review—an unusual move that pushes the arch significantly closer to final approval
It may get that in November from the National Capital Planning Commission, another federal body that has rubber-stamped several of Trump’s building projects in D.C
Trump initially made little secret of the actual purpose of the arch, which will rise above Memorial Circle, a traffic roundabout between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery

When a model of the structure was first spotted in the Oval Office last October, Trump told journalists that it was meant to honor “me.” After that, however, officials pitched it as a commemorative work for the nation’s 250th birthday

Later, in arguing against the veterans’ lawsuit, the project’s lead agency, the National Park Service, said the arch did not need congressional approval because a 1925 law had already authorized a pair of columns on that end of Memorial Bridge, to symbolize the post–Civil War reconciliation of North and South

Then, on Sunday, Trump invoked national security, announcing that the structure would house ammunition, drones, and snipers. “There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Out of the 59 top cities and Capitals, Washington, D.C., IS THE ONLY ONE IN THE WORLD THAT DOES NOT HAVE A TRIUMPHAL ARCH, but it will now and, by far, the greatest of them all!” A White House official told me that the arch would include military infrastructure while also remaining open to the public, and that the newly announced features do not alter the design or review process
The National Park Service and Interior Department did not respond to my questions about the project
If changing the purpose of the arch was meant to speed construction, it could have precisely the opposite effect
The project was already in its final stages of approval, the pesky matter of the lawsuit notwithstanding
But Trump’s plan to deck out the arch with weapons is likely to involve more agencies, lead to more litigation, and—this might be the important part to Trump—create further delays

On Thursday, the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation announced it had ended the arch’s routine consultation process—known as Section 106—after the National Park Service concluded that it was unlikely to produce an agreement with outside parties providing feedback on the proposal

Although this process isn’t legally binding, officials undertake it for federal construction projects that could affect historic properties, and proponents say it forces agencies to evaluate the effects of their projects and allows the public to have a say
In this case, it took months before officials ended the process early

Outside parties are supposed to give feedback during the review, but Charles Birnbaum, founder of the Cultural Landscape Foundation, told me his group and other consulting parties were invited to only one meeting

Just days before the president’s announcement on Sunday, Park Service officials sent the consulting groups a proposed memorandum of agreement that acknowledged the arch would unavoidably harm surrounding historic properties, but that concluded the project would move forward as planned
Because the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation has now canceled this process altogether, it will prepare its own formal comments and seek approval from Interior Secretary Doug Burgum
That timeline means that the Trump administration could bring the arch before the National Capital Planning Commission in November

Sara Bronin, a former chair of the ACHP and a professor at the George Washington University Law School, told me that termination of consultation is very unusual and reserved for cases in which parties who have diligently worked to resolve a project’s adverse effects still fail to come to an agreement

During her year as chair, she said, she exercised that authority only one time (for a wind-energy project). “By prematurely terminating consultation on the Triumphal Arch proposed by President Trump, the ACHP and interim chair Travis Voyles are making a farce of the Section 106 process,” she wrote me in an email. “True consultation has never occurred for the Triumphal Arch, and it looks like the Park Service and ACHP will bend over backwards to avoid it.” [ Read: The rush-job presidency ] In theory, Bronin said, the arch’s expansion to include national-security infrastructure should actually trigger a new Section 106 process
Previously, the National Park Service determined that the structure would adversely affect historic properties
But that analysis was conducted for a triumphal arch—not a military facility
Greg Werkheiser, an attorney at Cultural Heritage Partners and a plaintiff in a lawsuit to stop Trump’s plans to paint the Dwight D

Eisenhower Executive Office Building, said the changing function makes the arch a fundamentally different undertaking from the one preservationist groups have reviewed. “That’s likely to be a legal problem,” he told me in an email

All of this comes after ACHP announced plans to water down the historic-preservation rules that have applied to the arch—which could mean that the next time the Trump administration wants to erect a new monument, it faces less red tape to begin with
The process for creating new monuments in Washington, D.C., is well understood

But adding drones and ammo to one is a new wrinkle. “There’s no American monument that’s ever been used for that on a permanent basis,” Bryan Clark Green, a former member of the National Capital Planning Commission, told me

If the arch is to double as a military facility, Green said, the government would need to rethink how people and vehicles enter the site, how military personnel move through the structure, and how the public is kept away from sensitive operations
All of those considerations would require major revisions that would bring the project back before the National Capital Planning Commission and the Commission on Fine Art

Green told me the new arch plans should also trigger another review from the Federal Aviation Administration, which released a final report a week ago determining that the structure “would not pose a hazard to aircraft” even though it sits near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport
Along with the “eternal flame,” floodlights have been ordered by the agency to illuminate the structure
The FAA did not respond to questions I sent the agency
The bureaucratic requirements won’t end there
Military construction ordinarily follows its own yearslong planning and budgeting process, involving the Pentagon, the White House, and Congress

Mark Cancian, a retired Marine Corps colonel who oversaw military-construction budgets for the federal government, told me that he would expect the Department of Defense to contribute at least some money toward military-use portions of the arch—which was already estimated to have a $100 million price tag

title: Why Democrats stopped talking about climate
excerpt: Michigan Democratic congressional candidate Will Lawrence speaks with reporters on September 14, 2026, in Mason, Michigan. | Nic Antaya/Getty Images William Law
body: Michigan Democratic congressional candidate Will Lawrence speaks with reporters on September 14, 2026, in Mason, Michigan. | Nic Antaya/Getty Images William Lawrence is a Democrat running to represent Michigan’s Lansing-area Seventh Congressional District with a campaign that largely focuses on data centers and affordability

It’s not an unusual story in 2026 — but not long ago, Lawrence was cutting his teeth in progressive politics as a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, primarily focused on organizing around the climate crisis

His arc, from progressive activist to politician, is emblematic of a bigger trend, as a wave of millennial progressives in midterm races across the country try to lean into issues that have broader, more immediate appeal with voters
But that arc also raises big questions about the left’s changing priorities

In a recent interview for Vox’s podcast and video series America, Actually , host Astead Herndon spoke with Lawrence about his past activism and how he has pivoted. “It can sometimes feel like…folks hop from issue to issue, whether it’s climate, even anti-AI right now, without those things being solved,” Herndon told Lawrence
According to Lawrence, “that’s the reality of the time

It seems like everything is unraveling, and it is because the whole social, economic, political compact is being renegotiated, not just in this country, but on a global stage.” Still, Lawrence said, that earlier organizing shapes how he sees different challenges today

The two also discussed whether opposition to data centers and AI has wide, regular-voter appeal in places like Michigan and how Lawrence went from hopeless and disengaged to regaining a sense of agency through organizing
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel

You started in Sunrise and were at the forefront of a young progressive movement that was aligned at that time — in 2018, 2019, and I think still — with progressive members of Congress like Rashida Tlaib or Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
I remember reporting about Sunrise at the time
The goal was to elect a Bernie Sanders, but the other goal was to have the party largely embrace things like a Green New Deal
How would you grade the efforts of the climate movement of that time, looking back? I think we did some things very well
We put climate jobs and justice at the top of the agenda for the incoming Biden administration
I think the Bernie-Biden task force is an often overlooked but very important chapter of that whole story, where Bernie and Biden both understood they had to bring their people to the table
And that’s how Build Back Better got negotiated
We fought hard for Build Back Better , and ultimately came up two votes shy in the United States Senate

Do you see that as a success or a failure of the climate movement? I think Build Back Better was a success in coming to the table and negotiating, from the Green New Deal to Build Back Better, and then what we ended up with was the Inflation Reduction Act after it passed the final filter, which was Sen
At the time, now, how I felt about it was, this is historic
This is the largest investment in green jobs and infrastructure in United States history
I’m tremendously proud of the work that I did and so many others did
Just in my district alone, we’ve delivered $26 billion in investment for manufacturing and sustainability because of the Inflation Reduction Act
But at the time, we knew that this is maybe 5 percent or 10 percent of what we need in scope
And now we’re experiencing the consequences of that
Obviously, we still have a very volatile economy
We still lack energy security because we now have closed the Strait of Hormuz
We’re still too dependent on a global oil market, and we could use many more investments in solar and other kinds of renewable energy than we have now
And ultimately, it wasn’t enough for the Biden-Harris administration to be able to win reelection, because people didn’t feel it enough in their pocketbooks
Why do you think Democrats are talking less about climate? I think it’s the intensity of the crises that we face

It feels like we’re falling through midair, after the end of all of the constitutional protections, the rule of law, and the economic security that people had previously enjoyed.  There are a lot of very acute and urgent crises, and I think that that has bumped climate, which is a super massive but also somewhat slow-moving crisis, a little bit lower on the priority list just in terms of what comes up for people on the Hill
You went back to Michigan to focus on housing and advocacy

Did that make you think a little differently about the national work you were doing? I think it’s fair to say that when I was younger, I got very focused on this climate issue, and I was very focused on it because it is this existential crisis we all face
But it was after the pandemic that I wanted to bring my work closer to home
I wanted to do the work of putting down roots in the place that had raised me and make my life there

And in seeking to organize there, it was clear that we needed an in to organize that was more immediate. “I believe in the agency of regular people taking charge of our own lives and working together to build a better future.” More immediate than the Green New Deal
Than the Green New Deal or than the looming climate crisis

People know that that’s an issue, but they’re like, “I’ve gotta pay rent at the end of the month.” And as an organizer, I believe that you have to listen to people, you have to hear what’s going on for them, and then work on issues that have the potential to bring people together
Whether you’re in the city of Lansing, whether you’re in small towns, urban, rural, suburban, young or old, everybody can agree that the rent is too damn high and it’s too hard to buy a home anymore
Were you surprised Trump won the state in 2024?  No

title: Inside a quest to learn about the ocean’s mysterious “deep reefs”
excerpt: An autonomous reef monitoring structure (ARMS) in the mesophotic zone. | © Luiz Rocha This story was originally published in  The Highlight
body: An autonomous reef monitoring structure (ARMS) in the mesophotic zone. | © Luiz Rocha This story was originally published in  The Highlight
To get access to member-exclusive stories like this every month,  become a Vox Member today
PALAU, Micronesia — On a bright, sunny day last May, I stood on a boat surrounded by the turquoise waters of the island nation of Palau
I was there in the western Pacific watching scuba divers as they prepared to bring up evidence of a mysterious aquatic world.  Palau is famous for its spectacular and rich coral reefs

But these divers were planning to descend past those sun-lit marine communities and down into a lesser-known twilight zone known as the “mesophotic coral ecosystems.”  Mesophotic essentially means “middle” and “light,” which is where these ecosystems are — not quite in the bright daylight, not quite in the profound darkness, but somewhere in between

For simplicity’s sake, we’ll call these communities, which range from some 30 meters to 150 meters below the surface, the “deep reefs.”  One of the divers on the boat with me was a zoologist and curator at the California Academy of Sciences named Luiz Rocha, who has spent decades studying these deep reefs and their secrets.  “Anything between 30 meters and 150 meters is really, really unknown,” he told me
Because these deep reefs are so unknown, researchers like Rocha are left with big questions

They want to get a baseline picture of what is going on in these ecosystems — even just who lives there! — so that they can better understand how they function.  They’ve also tried to work out whether ( or not ) these deep reefs might provide a refuge for species living in shallower coral reefs

I was in Palau for Vox’s Unexplainable podcast because, in an effort to gather more information about these mysterious places, Rocha left some scientific structures down in these twilight depths back in 2016
Those structures then spent almost a decade becoming encrusted with all kinds of marine life

And now, Rocha was back to retrieve them, hoping that he — along with many other scientists — would be able to open them up, like a box of scientific puzzle pieces, full of clues about this under-understood marine world

View Link So what is a mesophotic “deep reef”?  One thing that’s often acknowledged in papers about and descriptions of the “mesophotic coral ecosystems” is that scientists don’t know as much as they’d like to. A National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration article about them from 2019 is full of “may’s” as in: they may “serve as essential fish habitat for economically and ecologically important species.” Researchers do know some things, of course

They know that these deep reefs can be found in many of the same locations as shallower coral reefs — so mainly the tropical and subtropical parts of the world, like Micronesia , the Caribbean , and even the Gulf of Mexico
They’ve found that there are many species that seem to be unique to these places, and recent research points to their potential susceptibility to climate change
Researchers have also gotten a sense of some of the key differences between these deep reefs and their shallower coral neighbors
In shallow reefs, hard corals team up with photosynthesizing algaes

The algaes provide the corals with nutrients, and the corals secrete a calcium-carbonate matrix that helps create the architecture of the reef.  As you go deeper, though, the light begins to fade, and the opportunities for photosynthesis start to fade with it
So the animals living down in the deep reefs are the ones that can survive in a dimmer, cooler world

Why are these places so mysterious?  Scientists can dive into the deep reefs to try to learn more about these understudied places — as Rocha has — but exploring down at 100 meters requires more difficult, riskier technical diving than exploring at shallower depths

The deeper you dive, for example, the faster gasses get pushed into your tissues, which imposes limits on these really deep dives. “We have a very, very short time,” Rocha says, “And by short time, I mean five minutes

Six, seven minutes.”  Scientists might take some pictures in that time, or make some measurements, or collect a few samples, but then they have to move back upwards, a process which can take hours because they have to rise slowly to avoid decompression sickness
It is, obviously, not particularly efficient to study an ecosystem in five- to seven-minute bursts

People have also used remote operated vehicles and submersibles to explore the deep reefs, but those have their own issues, and cameras can’t always capture all the detail you might want, or photograph more secretive, cryptic animals

So huge gaps remain in scientific knowledge about these ecosystems.  “Whenever we go somewhere,” Rocha says, “the first thing we find is new species. … It’s the most basic thing in science you can do.” But this effort goes beyond just cataloguing new species of fish or sponges or sea slugs.  Rocha wants to answer seemingly fundamental questions like: What is the main energy source for everything down here in the dimmer light? What does the food chain look like? How have things evolved to live down at these depths? How similar are they to the shallow ecosystems, and how different? How are they affected by climate change — and what’s the most efficient way to protect them?  But, “in some ways we don’t even know what questions to ask,” Rocha says. “We really only know what questions to ask after we have a baseline understanding of what the ecosystem is

And for deep reefs, we don’t know that yet.”  A new way to understand the deep reefs using “prefab housing” Rocha is not deterred by the enormous number of question marks that surround these deep reefs

For years now, he has been gathering bits of basic information about them, often via those very short dives.  About a decade ago, though, Rocha got interested in another method for sampling the biodiversity of this sort of marine ecosystem — a technique involving “ autonomous reef monitoring structures ” (ARMS)
Basically, each ARMS is a stack of several PVC plates, separated at uniform intervals and attached to a base plate
They look like little grey, featureless hotels

You take them to a place that you want to study, bring them down, secure them, and then leave them alone for a while to let them collect…life. “As soon as you drop any kind of clean structure on a reef,” Rocha says, “it starts getting colonized by larvae of everything around it — of sponges, gorgonians, corals

And then, because there’s all a lot of hiding spots between the plates — so between the floors of the hotel — they start getting colonized by shrimp, by mollusks, by ascidians, by anything you can imagine in the ocean. … And it becomes this stable, diverse mini reef, if you will, packed with a lot of biodiversity that would be very hard to collect all at once in any given reef.” A few years after that initial drop, you come back, collect the ARMS, and then study the mini reef that has grown on them
You can sample and touch and analyze things to your heart’s content.  It’s not only a very effective way to collect lots of creatures, all at once, but also a great way to do so in a standardized way

If you went down — or sent a robot down — to collect an encrusted rock from a reef, you could learn a lot about the life on it, but it would be hard to compare the life on that rock to life on other rocks from other reefs, or even the same reef, because each rock would have its own unique characteristics

Not so for ARMS. “ Every one’s the same,” Chris Meyer, director of the Smithsonian Global ARMS program, told me, “It’s prefab housing, and then you just look to see who moves in.”  To Rocha, this seemed like a great way to get a really good, long look at the deep reefs instead of the brief glimpses he was getting from diving
It was also, he told me, fairly cheap to deploy them
So from 2016 to 2018, with some private funding, he and his colleagues left ARMS in some of the deep reefs around Palau — as well as in Guam, the Marshall Islands, and French Polynesia

They installed some around 50 meters, and some around 100, and then some around 10 meters, so he could compare the deep reefs to their shallower neighbors.  After that, he waited.  In fact, he waited a little longer than he would have liked, because the retrieval of ARMS is more expensive than deploying them, so he had to work out more funding.  Eventually, private funders agreed to underwrite the retrieval of the ARMS that Rocha had left
Which is how he and his fellow divers finally found themselves on a boat in Palau again, ready to pull up these structures for the deep
Opening the scientific puzzle box Over the course of a few days, I watched a whole team of people pull several ARMS out of the deep reefs of Palau
Some of the ARMS were relatively sparse, but others were almost fuzzy with organisms — vibrant with red and orange and green and pink and white
One had a massive sponge attached to it, another had several delicate fronds dangling from it like coralline ferns

title: The Pentagon wants $30 million to build an AI-powered lie detector
excerpt: The Pentagon wants a smarter lie detector: The Department of Defense is requesting $30.3 million over five years for "Polygraph+"—an AI-powered upgrade to tradi
body: The Pentagon wants a smarter lie detector: The Department of Defense is requesting $30.3 million over five years for "Polygraph+"—an AI-powered upgrade to traditional polygraph technology that could read physiological signals without touching the subject

The science still doesn't hold up: Polygraph technology has been repeatedly debunked since its invention in the 1920s, with a landmark government report calling the evidence for its accuracy "weak at best"—and experts warn AI adds uncertainty on top of an already invalid tool

There's no universal tell for lying: Researchers say the fundamental problem remains unsolved: There is no single physiological signal that reliably indicates deception in all people, making any technology built on that premise structurally flawed

Critics see intimidation, not investigation: Legal scholars warn that the real purpose may be less about catching liars and more about pressuring people to confess—particularly as the Pentagon ramps up polygraph use to hunt for press leakers under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. " data-chronoton-post-id="1145144" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> The US government wants to spend $30.3 million over the next five years on an improved form of lie detector, according to a Department of Defense budget request

The program, called Polygraph+ or Polygraph Next, will focus on scoring algorithms that use artificial intelligence and machine learning and on a technique called “standoff sensing,” which refers to the ability to take physiological readings without attaching a device to a subject’s person

According to details of the budget document, which were first reported by Inside Defense , the project will “modernize federal polygraph and credibility assessment technologies” to improve their accuracy and reliability

But the project may be just the latest in a long line of failed attempts to use technology to detect lies. “It’s a misguided effort to reduce the complex to something that is tangible,” says Kyri Kotsoglou, a legal scholar at Northumbria University in the UK who studies the use of polygraphs in the justice system
The move comes at a time of high tension within the department
Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has been increasingly turning to polygraph tests in an attempt to find the sources of alleged leaks to the press

In September, the New York Times reported that around 50 officers on the Joint Staff had been given polygraph tests after news coverage reported on the depletion of US weapons stockpiles in the war with Iran.  Polygraph+ will be run by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), which conducts background checks for the federal government

According to the budget document, which has not yet been approved by Congress, the new technology will be used for vetting of prospective employees and “insider threat detection.” It is not yet clear which specific technologies will be used, and the DCSA did not respond to a request for more information.  But other Pentagon efforts offer potential clues
In 2023, the department’s Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) ran an open submission process to find companies with products that could be used for deception detection

It selected two companies to build prototypes : Presage Technologies, which claims to be able to measure heart rate and breathing rate using standard cameras, and Altec Research, a medical sensor company now branching out into non-contact sensing technologies
A screenshot of Altec’s prototype technology released by the DIU shows that it tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity
Presage Technologies and Altec Research did not respond to requests for comment
The DIU declined to comment.  Altec Research has built a prototype that tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity
ALTEC RESEARCH Current lie detection technology has barely changed since the polygraph was invented in the 1920s
Examiners rely on blood pressure, pulse, breathing, and sweat measurements to determine if someone is lying

They make judgments about the veracity of respondents’ replies on the basis of differences in their physiological response to baseline questions like “Is the sky blue?” and target questions like “Have you ever committed a crime?” The federal government conducts tens of thousands of the tests each year while screening employees, but the reliability of this technology has been repeatedly challenged—and its results are rarely admissible in court

In 1983, Congress’s Office of Technology Assessment concluded that there was very limited evidence supporting the polygraph’s use for screening employees, and in 2003 , the US National Research Council (NRC) said evidence for its efficacy was “weak at best.”  Research suggests humans can spot a lie just over half the time without any technical assistance
The American Polygraph Association claims the polygraph is between 80% and 94% accurate
But the 2003 NRC report pointed out that a screening test with this level of accuracy could still lead to a lot of mistakes
The DOD employs 2.8 million people; an imperfect system applied at that scale could end up falsely accusing tens of thousands
Polygraph interpretations are often subjective: Different examiners get wildly different results , and people from minority groups are more likely to be judged as deceptive

What’s more, with training it’s possible for interviewees to learn a variety of countermeasures that can help beat the test; for example, they may artificially heighten their physiological response to baseline questions by stepping on a pin hidden in their shoe.  “If you know how it works, you can beat it,” says Sophie van der Zee, an associate professor who studies deception at Erasmus University in Rotterdam
She says the machine’s biggest effect is deterrence—often, subjects confess before it even begins. “But that only works if people think a polygraph works,” she points out
Various new strategies for lie detection have been attempted over the decades , with technologies ranging from thermal cameras to pupil trackers to brain scans
None of them have yielded reliable results outside the lab

The problem is that there’s no single telltale sign of lying that’s true for everyone all the time. “There is still no Pinocchio’s nose,” says van der Zee.  AI could theoretically improve polygraphs if it could find patterns in the data that examiners can’t
AI algorithms are also more likely to be used for “multi-modal” deception detection, which seeks to combine multiple measurements into an overall deception “score” that is harder for people to game

Three things are happening under the surface that lie detection tries to home in on, van der Zee says: physiological stress, cognitive load, and the conscious efforts people make to conceal the fact that they’re lying
Current polygraph technology tackles only one. “The more you can have combined methods that approach it from these three different angles, the more successful you will be,” van der Zee says
This isn’t a new concept—in the 2000s, researchers at Manchester Metropolitan University in the UK developed a system called Silent Talker that generated a deception score from video footage
This was later folded into iBorderCtrl, an EU-funded pilot program
In the US, a project called AVATAR incorporated eye tracking, voice analysis, and body movement detection into a tool for use at border crossings
All these projects have quietly faded away.  Kotsoglou says combining AI and the polygraph is “the worst of both worlds” because it adds uncertainty on top of invalidity

Even if AI or machine learning can spot previously unseen patterns in physiological data, it won’t be able to reliably link them to lying because there is no real ground truth.  “Even if you have all the records in the world from polygraph tests, you don’t know whether those polygraph tests are right or not,” says Marion Oswald, a professor of law who has written with Kotsoglou on the use of polygraphs in the justice system

She fears that new forms of lie detection will, like the polygraph, be used more as a psychological prop than a scientific tool.  “It seems very much a response to the concern of the current administration to leaks and perceived lack of loyalty,” says Oswald. “[Lie detection is] being used as a threat, to intimidate and force people to confess to things, as opposed to anything that’s actually getting valid information.”

title: Young organs may not be a fountain of youth for recipients
excerpt: Young hearts don't stay young for long: New research shows that transplanted hearts quickly take on the biological age of whoever receives them — meaning a
body: Young hearts don't stay young for long: New research shows that transplanted hearts quickly take on the biological age of whoever receives them — meaning a 30-year-old heart given to a 70-year-old recipient will soon "act" 70

The body's environment calls the shots: Researchers found that neither the recipient's blood nor other organs were meaningfully affected by the donor heart's age, suggesting the body's broader environment overpowers any rejuvenating potential a young organ might carry

A silver lining for transplant medicine: The findings could push surgeons to stop discarding older donor hearts, since biological age appears to reset after transplant anyway — potentially expanding a critically short supply of viable organs

Immortality remains out of reach: The study underscores just how stubbornly complex aging is — reversing it entirely would require unwinding DNA damage, structural decay, and cellular wear across every tissue simultaneously, which scientists say is an enormous, likely impossible, challenge. " data-chronoton-post-id="1145083" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Around this time last year I was attending an aging conference in Manchester, listening to a talk about fly aging, when my phone started pinging

News outlets were reporting that a hot mic had caught Russia’s and China’s leaders discussing the possibility of living forever . “With the developments of biotechnology, human organs can be continuously transplanted, and people can live younger and younger, and even achieve immortality,” Russia’s Vladimir Putin reportedly told China’s Xi Jinping
He seems to have been referring to the “replacement” theory of longevity, which has been supported by multiple experiments that involved physically stitching young mice to old ones
Something about the young blood rejuvenated the old mice
Perhaps young organs could rejuvenate world leaders in their 70s, too
Unfortunately for Putin, new research pours a little cold water on this idea
Studies on transplanted hearts in both mice and humans suggest that new hearts soon adopt the biological age of the recipient, no matter how young they were to begin with
The finding could be important for transplantation, but it also highlights just how complex aging—and rejuvenation—are
Jesse Poganik at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston is one of the many scientists trying to understand exactly what it is about the bodies of young mice that rejuvenates old ones
Plenty of research has focused on seeking the secrets of youth in young blood
But what if it’s something about young organs instead? To find out, he and his colleagues performed a set of heart transplants in mice

In humans, heart transplants typically involve removing a damaged or injured heart and replacing it with another from a donor who is usually much younger than the recipient. (When Poganik assessed hospital records, he found that most recipients were about 20 years older than their donors.) The mouse transplants were different: Mice received a second heart, implanted in the neck—a procedure that’s slightly simpler and allows scientists to compare the new hearts with the existing ones
In some cases, young adult mice were given a heart from a middle-aged donor
In others, middle-aged mice got young hearts
The team used a trio of “aging clocks” —molecular tools used to estimate the biological ages of tissues and whole organisms—to assess whether the additional hearts affected the mice in any way
These clocks were good at predicting the chronological age of mice that didn’t get new hearts
Poganik says he was expecting to see a reciprocal effect, and that young hearts might benefit older animals, for example
In previous work by other members of his team, young mice that got old hearts experienced a buildup of senescent cells in their other organs
These cells are thought to contribute to the aging process, suggesting that receiving an old organ might prematurely age an animal
When he and his colleagues analyzed the transplanted hearts between four and six months after surgery, they found that the hearts seemed to have adopted the biological age of the recipients
Young hearts got older, and old hearts got younger. “The environment of the transplanted organ really dictates how it seems to behave biologically,” he says
The findings were published online at bioRxiv last week

The team also looked at each mouse’s blood and other organs—including its original heart—and were surprised to find that they seemed to be unaffected by the presence of the new heart, despite the age of its donor
The finding was backed up by data from human heart transplants
People who receive a donor heart must typically undergo a series of heart biopsies after surgery
The tiny pieces of heart tissue collected from people who had heart transplants at Brigham and Women’s have been stored for decades

And when Poganik and his colleagues tested their biological ages with the aging clocks, they found a similar pattern: No matter the age of the donor, a new heart quickly adopts the biological age of the person who received it

It’s not clear why this is, but João Pedro de Magalhães, who studies aging at the University of Birmingham in the UK and was not involved in the study, thinks it might have something to do with the recipient’s immune system
Perhaps immune cells circulating in the blood might affect markers of aging in the new organ, he says
Perhaps the potential rejuvenating effects of a young heart end up being diluted by all the other aged components of an older body, Poganik suggests
Or maybe a single organ just isn’t enough to see an effect

Poganik hopes his finding will encourage surgeons to consider using hearts from older donors, many of which are discarded on the assumption they won’t function as well. (Machines used to preserve organs before transplantation are changing that already—and Poganik has worked on another study showing that these devices seem to rejuvenate donor livers to some extent.) But the study also highlights just how complicated aging is

If organs seem to be getting older by one measure but not by another, how can we get a full picture of the biological age of an organ, or a person? This complexity means that scientists are not likely to discover a true way to completely reverse aging, says Poganik. “That would mean that every aspect of aging has to go back in time,” he says

Reversing DNA damage, structural damage, and all the other degradations that are part of the aging package, across all our various cells and tissues, presents an enormous challenge. “There are aspects of biological age that are probably reversible, and there are aspects that are probably not,” he says

<p>A concrete slab is slowly lowered into place in order to complete a section of the wall. Inch by inch, the vibrant, hilly Palestinian community on the other side gets smaller and smaller. </p>

<p>And then – just like that – a world that’s a stone’s throw away is gone. </p>

<p><a href="https://edinburghuniversitypress.com/book-israel-palestine.html">As someone</a> <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/arrested-movement-in-the-middle-east-9780755656721/">who studies</a> the restrictions placed on Palestinians, I often think about this scene as a microcosm of Israel’s decades-long use of walls, checkpoints and surveillance technologies to seal off Palestinians from the rest of society.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A huge slab of concrete approaches another slab with a small opening of the community on the other side visible." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761806/original/file-20260923-60-s6lwrz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761806/original/file-20260923-60-s6lwrz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=372&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761806/original/file-20260923-60-s6lwrz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=372&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761806/original/file-20260923-60-s6lwrz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=372&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761806/original/file-20260923-60-s6lwrz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=468&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761806/original/file-20260923-60-s6lwrz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=468&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761806/original/file-20260923-60-s6lwrz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=468&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A still from the 2004 documentary ‘Wall’ depicts the moment that a section of the West Bank barrier is completed.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5iyA31Tw-7I">Down The Rabbit Hole/YouTube</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Nowhere is this dynamic more evident than the Gaza Strip, which Israel <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/45406228">fenced in during the 1990s</a> and has <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2214163">blockaded since 2007</a>, citing security concerns and the threat of militant attacks.</p>

<p>Thanks to these barriers, the immense suffering of Palestinians in Gaza – <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cvgpd1x00exo">more than 70,000</a> of whom have been killed as a result of the Israel-Hamas war since 2023 – has been difficult to document. The Israeli government largely bars international journalists from entering the Gaza Strip independently, while Palestinians in Gaza are generally not allowed to leave the Gaza Strip.</p>

<p>But the Sept. 10, 2026, premiere of Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s film “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt44766123/">NAZA</a>” at the Venice International Film Festival has put the spotlight on the ongoing tragedy in Gaza without relying on footage of gruesome corpses or bombed-out neighborhoods. </p>

<p>The film consists largely of anonymous testimony from 24 members of Israel’s military and intelligence services. They discuss the ways in which <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/11/naza-directors-film-israeli-intelligence-rachel-szor-yuval-abraham-">Israel has used artificial intelligence</a> to target Hamas officials, despite knowing the attacks will also generate large numbers of civilian casualties. The title, “NAZA,” comes from an acronym for the Hebrew phrase “nezek agavi,” or “collateral damage,” and it’s the Israeli military’s threshold system for how many civilian casualties are acceptable in its military strikes on Gaza since <a href="https://www.cfr.org/global-conflict-tracker/conflict/israeli-palestinian-conflict">the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks</a>. Hamas-led militants from Gaza launched those attacks in southern Israel, murdering 1,200 people – mostly civilians – and also taking about 250 hostages.</p>

<p>To me, part of the film’s power lies in its focus on the clinical way of carrying out strikes on Gaza from a distance. But the Israeli military’s approach could only work after systematically isolating the Palestinian people over the course of decades.</p>

<h2>Unseen victims</h2>

<p>In addition to constructing walls and blockading Gaza, Israel has enforced separation of Palestinians <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/14650045.2011.562944">by restricting or denying permits</a> to Palestinians wishing to enter or work in Israel through <a href="https://www.versobooks.com/products/2007-hollow-land">aerial surveillance</a> and <a href="https://www.versobooks.com/products/2007-hollow-land">through the expansion</a> of Israeli settlements in the West Bank.  </p>

<p>Both the visual language and the content of “NAZA” reflect and reveal how knowledge of Palestinian suffering is often mitigated in Israeli culture, politics and daily life. </p>

<p>The film juxtaposes audio of Israeli soldiers’ testimony with shots of the Tel Aviv cityscape at night. In these interviews, the soldiers map out how targets are chosen, how attacks are planned and how much leeway is given for civilian casualties. </p>

<p>The victims themselves are largely unseen, despite their close proximity: Tel Aviv sits a mere 43 miles – or 70 kilometers – up the coast from the Gaza Strip. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Photograph of cityscape with buildings destroyed by bombs and makeshift tents set up." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762121/original/file-20260924-50-tyn04k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762121/original/file-20260924-50-tyn04k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762121/original/file-20260924-50-tyn04k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762121/original/file-20260924-50-tyn04k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762121/original/file-20260924-50-tyn04k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762121/original/file-20260924-50-tyn04k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762121/original/file-20260924-50-tyn04k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Gaza City, shown on Sept. 21, 2026, is just 43 miles from Tel Aviv, yet the two can seem worlds apart.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/view-shows-makeshift-tents-set-up-amidst-damaged-buildings-news-photo/2295916095?adppopup=true">Faiz Qreqa/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The choice to film primarily at night, in darkness, using disembodied voices to tell a story not depicted on camera, further highlights the extent to which these events have been obscured in Israel and around the world. Perhaps that’s why the Israeli government has gone to such great lengths to discredit the film, saying it contains “<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/14/gaza-documentary-makers-naza-israel-citizenship-ntwnfb?">deliberate distortions of reality</a>.” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/14/world/middleeast/israel-naza-documentary-backlash.html">has threatened to revoke the citizenship of its directors</a>. </p>

<p>In response to the interest and backlash surrounding the film, <a href="https://x.com/yuval_abraham/status/2103061893913162054">the filmmakers announced</a> that “NAZA” will be available to stream for free, for anyone to see, beginning in November 2026.</p>

<h2>Breaking through</h2>

<p>“NAZA” highlights a psychological distance between attacker and attacked that was enabled by AI, computer screens and the physical isolation of the targets. Yet it is far from the first film to call attention to the invisibility of Palestinians.</p>

<p>Elia Suleiman’s 2002 dark comedy “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0274428/">Divine Intervention</a>” repeatedly stages scenes in which Palestinian characters are stuck at or try to get around an Israeli military checkpoint. And Yoav Shamir’s 2003 documentary “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0391857/">Checkpoint</a>” chronicles everyday interactions between Palestinians and Israeli soldiers at checkpoints in the West Bank and Gaza. </p>

<p>Other films center on acts of transgression or protest. Hany Abu-Assad’s 2013 drama “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2852406/">Omar</a>” and Ameen Nayfeh’s 2020 drama “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt12246266/">200 Meters</a>” both feature Palestinian characters who break the law and surreptitiously cross the West Bank border into Israeli territory, exposing themselves to physical and legal danger.</p>

<p>“<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt30953759/">No Other Land</a>” – the 2024 documentary <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-palestinian-israeli-film-just-won-an-oscar-so-why-is-it-so-hard-to-see-249233">that netted Abraham and Szor an Oscar</a>, along with fellow directors Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal – points the camera on Palestinian protest movements against land expropriations and home demolitions in the West Bank. In the 2011 film “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2125423/">5 Broken Cameras</a>,” Palestinian farmer Emad Burnat captures his West Bank village’s struggle against the construction of a massive wall that chokes off farmland and access to vital resources. Even as his cameras are repeatedly damaged or destroyed, Burnat refuses to stop documenting the resistance.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/40KW6knYMo4?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">‘NAZA’ will be available to stream for free starting in November 2026.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Crying while shooting</h2>

<p>“NAZA” also points to another phenomenon: how isolation and separation encourage complicity. The physical distance between Israeli soldiers and the people they target may make it easier to go along with or ignore what is happening.</p>

<p>In this way, “NAZA” grapples with a trope in Israeli films and literature of exploring the guilt of Israeli soldiers. Sometimes derisively referred to by critics as “<a href="https://academic.oup.com/screen/article-abstract/54/1/44/1623426">shooting and crying</a>,” the thematic framework of these films has been criticized for focusing on Israeli moral anguish at the expense of Palestinian experiences and perspectives.</p>

<p>For example, S. Yizhar’s 1949 novel, “Khirbet Khizeh,” which was adapted <a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0151202/">into a film</a> in 1978, tells the story from the perspective of Micha, an Israeli soldier fighting in the 1948 war that established the state of Israel. He’s part of a squad that expels Palestinians from their village, and his ensuing guilt provokes a crisis of conscience that haunts him for years to come. </p>

<p>Decades later, the 2008 animated documentary “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1185616/">Waltz With Bashir</a>” follows the film’s director, Ari Folman, as he plumbs his repressed memories of his participation in the <a href="https://www.npr.org/2007/08/28/12744311/timeline-1982-siege-of-beirut">1982 Israeli invasion of Beirut</a> and how he inadvertently helped Lebanese Christian Phalangist militia fighters carry out <a href="https://imeu.org/resources/resources/explainer-the-sabra-shatila-massacre/113">massacres of Palestinians at the Sabra and Shatila refugee camps</a>.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/uWo8U5J0XeY?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">‘Waltz With Bashir’ centered on the fragmented memories, trauma and guilt of an Israeli soldier who had helped facilitate the Sabra and Shatila massacre in Beirut, Lebanon, in 1982.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The “shooting and crying” genre was largely accepted in mainstream Israeli culture, with “Khirbet Khizeh” <a href="https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/1/article/963600/summary">taught in Israeli schools</a> for decades. But the Israeli government’s hostile reaction to “NAZA” perhaps signals not only the growing intolerance of dissent in Israel, but also a <a href="https://contendingmodernities.nd.edu/global-currents/shooting-and-singing/">fading cultural and political concern</a> with the morality of Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory.</p>

<h2>Whose voices get heard</h2>

<p>The centering of Israeli perspectives in these earlier works – as well as in “NAZA” – also shows how violence against Palestinians can be given greater credence when it’s described by Israelis themselves. </p>

<p>Recent Palestinian narratives about Gaza, such as “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt32606918/">From Ground Zero</a>” and “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt43743832/">Thirteen in Gaza</a>,” have garnered <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2025/sep/09/from-ground-zero-stories-from-gaza-review-scenes-of-ordinary-life-in-extremis">some attention and praise</a> in <a href="https://deadline.com/2026/09/thirteen-gaza-trailer-father-daughter-palestinian-netpac-1237109243/">the film world</a>, but nowhere near the same amount as “NAZA” has in the weeks since its premiere.</p>

<p>Even “No Other Land,” which is centered on a Palestinian village, features an Israeli journalist and filmmaker, Abraham, documenting the protests and confronting Israeli soldiers, and may not have received the same acclaim if it had been made entirely by Palestinians. </p>

<p>Yet, despite these many barriers, Palestinians have never stopped finding ways to make themselves heard. In addition to films like “Omar” and “200 Meters,” videos and images <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/14781158.2024.2415908">shared directly to social media</a> have allowed Palestinians to connect directly with audiences and shape global awareness of their plight, especially since the current war in Gaza began. </p>

<p>They have been able to bypass the physical barriers that have long restricted their movement – and the cultural barriers that have often kept their experiences out of sight.</p>

<title>Trump has gotten rid of many of the checks and balances that could stop him from demolishing the Kennedy Center</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762129/original/file-20260924-50-s3fk78.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C4000&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Musicians perform during a rally against the closing of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on Sept. 18, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Trump%20Kennedy%20Center/d0e3631e03724912b6556e5ffb0b4d5c/photo">AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Who gets to decide the future of the <a href="https://www.kennedy-center.org/memorial/">living memorial to former President John F. Kennedy</a>, and who holds those decision-makers to account?</p>

<p>This debate is becoming ever more fraught. A <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/17/us/politics/trump-kennedy-center-photos.html">photo taken on Sept. 16, 2026</a>, showed President Donald J. Trump in Air Force One reviewing a poster with the words “Kennedy Center DEMOLISH …” that many interpreted to mean “demolished.”</p>

<p>The image spread quickly. Like the protests that brought <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/protesters-plan-form-human-chain-kennedy-center-amid/story?id=136558872">throngs of arts lovers to the center a few days later</a>, it amplified the drama around the fate of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C. For more than a half-century, the multivenue complex has featured world-class symphonies, operas, dance and theater performances, along with education programs. </p>

<p>Whether it would be <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/17/arts/music/kennedy-center-closure-emergency-hearing.html">open or closed</a> to the public, active or dormant, repaired or dismantled, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/13/arts/design/trump-kennedy-center-bankruptcy-closure.html">solvent or bankrupt</a> and if it can <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/09/15/trump-kennedy-center-judge/a43ae64a-b123-11f1-92c2-5c918f4a6127_story.html">include Trump’s name in its branding</a> have been the subjects of widespread dispute and speculation since Trump returned to office.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://www.american.edu/cas/faculty/eataylor.cfm">professor and scholar of arts management</a>, I can explain why the official answers to who gets to decide and who is supposed to hold those deciders accountable are reasonably clear.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
